item.title: Fake VPN and 7-Zip Apps Turn Victims Into Residential Proxy Nodes
item.description:
"Lurking Lizard" ran a covert residential proxy business since 2022, enrolling victim devices via trojanized 7-Zip and WireVPN apps without consent, with over 1 million Android downloads.
Key findings:
- The attack chain starts with typosquat domains like 7zip[.]com (vs. the real 7-zip[.]org) delivering trojanized installers. The fake 7-Zip drops hero.exe and uphero.exe into C:\Windows\SysWOW64\hero. WireVPN, the evolved rebrand, mirrors this exactly: wire.exe and upwire.exe in C:\Windows\SysWOW64\wire. Same skeleton, new label.
- A hardcoded IPLogger beacon at hxxps://iplogger[.]com/mnWD appeared across multiple payloads spanning years, tying fake 7-Zip, WireVPN, and fake TikTok/YouTube tools to one operator. Lurking Lizard used a legitimate third-party tracker to avoid hosting their own C2 telemetry.
- WireVPN is signed with a valid certificate issued to WEILAI NETWORK TECHNOLOGY CO., LIMITED. Network behavior exposes it: rather than a single stable VPN tunnel, it pings large numbers of distributed IPs and maintains multiple concurrent connections, classic proxy-node behavior, not privacy-tool behavior.
- Infoblox mapped 230+ domains including smartproxy[.]org and proxyreviews[.]org back to this actor via shared DNS, hosting, and WHOIS data. WHOIS registration points toward China 🇨🇳 (Wuhan area codes, registrant names including Cheng Li variants).
Hunt C:\Windows\SysWOW64\wire and \hero for unsigned or anomalously signed executables.

item.title: Detection Engineering in the Era of Semantic Malware
item.description:
Brainworm and the promptware kill chain are forcing detection engineers to rebuild core assumptions. Signatures, process trees, and network indicators all degrade when the attacker writes English, not assembly.
- Brainworm (Origin, March 2026) is a PoC that poisons CLAUDE.md with natural language C2 instructions over RabbitMQ/AMQP. No binary, no shellcode. The agent runtime executes malicious tool calls indistinguishable from legitimate ones. Researchers formalized 36 incidents (2023-early 2026) showing promptware now routinely achieves persistence, C2, lateral movement, and exfiltration across Claude Code, Cursor, Devin, and Slack AI.
- Memory config files are the new registry Run key. Alert on any modification to CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, AGENTS.md, or GEMINI.md by a process other than a known IDE or git operation, especially diffs containing URLs, shell commands, or base64 not in the last reviewed commit.
- Behavioral baselining is non-optional. You cannot signature-match non-deterministic tool call sequences, but you can baseline write-to-read ratios, session duration, and first-seen external destinations per agent session. Composite deviation across multiple fields is your signal, not any single indicator.
- Context window telemetry is the highest-value instrumentation gap: no major agent framework currently emits structured logs of what was loaded into the context window at inference time.

item.title: Hindsight 2026.06
item.description:
Hindsight v2026.06 adds Firefox support and deeper download forensics, making it a stronger cross-browser artifact parser for investigations.
Key updates:
- Firefox is now parsed alongside Chromium browsers. All profiles from all browsers merge into a single Timeline tab in XLSX output, with unified row types (url, cookie, autofill) so investigators can filter cross-browser activity in one view without stitching sources manually.
- Service Workers are parsed for the first time in Hindsight. Data comes from the Service Workers\Database LevelDB, which means historical and deleted records surface (shown as gray rows). A new Service Workers tab organizes origin, registration, and resources hierarchically.
- Downloads parsing is significantly expanded. Hindsight now reads shared_proto_db alongside the History DB, surfacing fields like download_source, request_headers, fetched_via_service_worker, and storage_partition. Critically, a new download (opened) row logs last_access_time when a user opened a file through the browser, a useful user-activity timestamp.
- The Extensions tab is now hierarchical: name, ID, and install info at the top level, with permissions and scripts nested below, improving readability during extension-abuse investigations.
Takeaway: update to v2026.06 via pip install pyhindsight or the GitHub release. On cross-browser cases, the merged Timeline tab is now your first stop.

item.title: UNC6692 and the SNOW Malware Ecosystem
item.description:
UNC6692 deploys the SNOW malware ecosystem via Microsoft Teams helpdesk impersonation, chaining email bombing, credential harvesting, and LSASS dumping to fully compromise a domain controller.
Key details:
- UNC6692 opened with an email bombing campaign to create user panic, then pivoted to Microsoft Teams (T1566.002) posing as IT helpdesk, directing victims to a fake "Mailbox Repair" portal on attacker-controlled AWS S3. The portal harvested credentials through repeated fake auth prompts and exfiltrated them to an actor S3 bucket (T1567.002).
- An AutoHotkey binary and script (T1059.010) with identical filenames auto-executed on download, deploying SNOWBELT, a malicious Chromium extension (T1176.001) masquerading as a heartbeat monitor. SNOWBELT pulled down SNOWGLAZE, SNOWBASIN, and Python utilities, then anchored persistence via a Startup folder shortcut (T1547.001) and scheduled tasks (T1053.005) launching hidden Edge processes while clearing security logs.
- SNOWGLAZE establishes WebSocket C2 tunnels (T1572) with SOCKS proxy support (T1090) through Heroku-hosted infrastructure. SNOWBASIN runs as a local HTTP server on port 8000, executing commands via cmd and PowerShell (T1059.003/001) and capturing screenshots (T1113).
- Lateral movement used PsExec over port 135 (T1021.002) and RDP through the SNOWGLAZE tunnel (T1021.001) to reach a backup server, where LSASS was dumped via Task Manager (T1003.001).

item.title: Helix, a New Name in the Data Extortion Ecosystem?
item.description:
"Helix" data extortion group uses vishing, device code phishing, and automated SharePoint exfiltration in a campaign tied to the BlackFile and ShinyHunters ecosystem, confirmed across multiple targets.
Key findings:
- Helix's kill chain starts with vishing that spoofs the target's actual manager by name, then walks victims into a device code phishing flow via oskeysync[.]com (registered through NICENIC, same registrar used by BlackFile and ShinyHunters). No credential is ever spoken. The result is a captured session token that bypasses Conditional Access entirely.
- Persistence is a single MFA Authenticator registration, completed within minutes of first sign-in from the same residential proxy geo-matched to the target's city. No malware, no OAuth grants, no service principals. The only artifact is a legitimate MFA entry in Entra ID logs.
- Exfiltration fingerprint is consistent: python-requests/2.28.1 user-agent, contentclass:STS_Site SharePoint enumeration, then bulk download, all from 179.43.185[.]230 (AS 51852, Private Layer INC), four addresses from confirmed BlackFile IP 179.43.185[.]226.
- Dwell varied from under one hour to over a week. The actor rotated 15+ residential IPs per mailbox and, in at least one case, tested containment 30-40 minutes after account disable by attempting MFA re-registration.
Disable device code authentication in Entra ID now.

item.title: Telegram-Hosted RedWing Malware Lets Anyone Rent Android Spyware Tools
item.description:
RedWing Android MaaS sold via Telegram lets novice attackers deploy full-featured banking spyware with zero coding skill, linked to Russian 🇷🇺 threat actors and the Oblivion malware family.
- RedWing is a commercial-grade subscription service distributed through Telegram, complete with operator documentation, tutorial videos, a referral discount program, and a bot that generates custom obfuscated APKs on demand. Fake storefronts mimic Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Huawei AppGallery with convincing ratings and reviews to drive installs.
- Post-install, a sequential permission flow coerces victims into disabling battery optimization, setting the app as default SMS handler, and enabling Accessibility Service, framed as routine setup. This gives the malware credential-overlay capability, OTP interception, real-time keylogging, and PIN/CVV scraping directly off the screen.
- Silent call forwarding is enabled via carrier code 21, redirecting all inbound calls to an attacker-controlled number and neutralizing phone-based 2FA and bank fraud callbacks in one step. Remote camera/mic activation uses take_photo and start_recording commands via the MediaRecorder API, with server-configurable recording duration.
- Zimperium identified 82 targeted institutions, heavily weighted toward Russian 🇷🇺 financial firms. Infected devices can also be conscripted into a DDoS botnet via the operator control panel.

item.title: GhostApproval: A Trust Boundary Gap in AI Coding Assistants
item.description:
GhostApproval: a symlink-following flaw (CWE-61 plus CWE-451 UI deception) hits 6 major AI coding assistants, enabling pre-authorization RCE on developer machines via malicious git repos.
- The attack is trivial: a repo contains a symlink disguised as a workspace file (e.g., project_settings.json -> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys). When a developer asks their AI assistant to "set up the workspace," the agent follows the symlink and writes an attacker SSH key outside the sandbox. No path canonicalization, no sandbox enforcement. Affected tools: Amazon Q Developer (CVE-2026-12958, fixed), Cursor (CVE-2026-50549, fixed), Google Antigravity (fixed), Anthropic Claude Code, Augment, and Windsurf.
- The deeper finding is CWE-451: in Claude Code, the agent's internal reasoning explicitly identified "this is a symbolic link to the Claude settings file," yet the confirmation prompt shown to the user read only "Make this edit to project_settings.json?" The human approved a lie. The Human-in-the-Loop became a rubber stamp.
- Windsurf and Amazon Q exhibited pre-authorization writes: the file was modified before the Accept/Reject dialog appeared. That dialog was an undo button, not a gate. Augment was worst: silent reads AND writes, no dialog at all, with the agent narrating the exfiltration in chat.
- Patch status at publication: AWS (language server 1.69.0), Cursor, and Google fixed. Augment acknowledged but no fix shipped. Windsurf acknowledged June 23, 2026, no update.

item.title: Spectra Analyze in Action: Hunting Device Code Phishing Pages
item.description:
Active Microsoft 365 device code phishing campaign abuses OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant flow to hijack accounts without stealing passwords, with 765 landing pages confirmed and new samples appearing within hours.
- Rather than spoofing a login page, this kit walks victims through a legitimate Microsoft authentication flow that silently authorizes an attacker-controlled device. No credential theft, no fake portal: the victim completes a real Microsoft prompt at aka[.]ms/devicelogin or login.microsoftonline[.]com/common/oauth2/deviceauth, and the attacker collects the resulting token.
- ReversingLabs published a YARA rule (authored by Malware Utkonos, dated 2026-05-20) targeting the HTML landing pages. Detection logic keys on Microsoft device login URLs, zero-width Unicode characters (ZWS E2808B, ZWNJ E2808C, WJ E281A0), a "dc=" JSON field, and a base64-encoded EVOSTS string. Files must be under 1MB.
- A retrohunt across the ReversingLabs corpus matched 765 samples, with the freshest appearing only hours before publication. The campaign is ongoing.
- Spectra Intelligence's URL crawler saves HTML response pages as first-class files, making it possible to hunt landing pages directly by source URL. Sample 87158731a98f30ff8a6280e5e14f094a402a861d is one confirmed landing page.

item.title: AI Security Incident – JadePuffer Ransomware Leverages AI Agent to Automate Attacks
item.description:
JadePuffer ransomware uses an LLM agent to autonomously execute a full attack chain, marking the first documented end-to-end agentic ransomware operation. Entry point was CVE-2025-3248 (CVSS 9.8, CISA KEV) in Langflow.
- CVE-2025-3248 is an unauthenticated RCE in Langflow's /api/v1/validate/code endpoint, patched April 2025 but still widely exposed. The agent delivered all payloads as Base64-encoded Python via that endpoint, then pivoted to a production MySQL/Nacos server by exploiting CVE-2021-29441 and forging JWTs with Nacos' publicly known default signing key.
- The LLM demonstrated real-time self-correction: after a bcrypt PATH failure broke a backdoor account, it autonomously diagnosed the issue, deleted the broken row, switched to direct bcrypt import, and logged in successfully, all within 31 seconds and zero human input.
- Encryption was irreversible by design. The agent ran AES_ENCRYPT() across 1,342 Nacos config items, dropped original tables, wrote ransom demands to a README_RANSOM table, then printed the AES key once to stdout without persisting it.
- Persistence artifact: a crontab heartbeat to attacker infrastructure every 30 minutes on the Langflow host.
Hunt your internet-exposed Langflow instances for unexpected crontab entries and outbound connections. Patch to 1.3.0+ immediately. Rotate any credentials stored in Langflow env vars. Sysdig captured 600+ payloads; full analysis in their report.

item.title: ClickFix to Cash-Out: Anatomy of a Mexican Banking-Fraud Toolkit
item.description:
REF6045 deploys SCMBANKER, an operator-assisted PowerShell banking-fraud toolkit targeting Mexico 🇲🇽's financial ecosystem via ClickFix fake-CAPTCHA lures, active since at least October 2025.
- Initial access uses fake CAPTCHA pages that copy a cmd.exe command to the clipboard, fetching validation.txt from open file servers (68.211.161[.]46, osogransd[.]online) and piping it directly to cmd.exe. The batch script launches Edge in kiosk mode pointing to fakeupdate[.]net as a distraction, loops UAC prompts every 20 seconds, and locks the mouse to a 1x1 pixel via user32.dll ClipCursor while bitsadmin bulk-downloads the toolkit to C:\Users\Public\.
- Persistence lands in two places: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run value "run" and run.vbs dropped to the Startup folder under %APPDATA%. A RunOnce key "id" writes the infection timestamp to C:\Users\Public\id.txt then self-deletes, giving responders a first-seen marker.
- The operator dashboard (C2: negratomasa2026[.]online and gestionmontelavaria2026[.]online) receives a beacon from cliente.ps1 every 30 seconds with hostname, GUID, internal/external IP, and RAT status. Banking sessions trigger jujuzkt.ps1, which fires screenshot bursts (~42 images per trigger via rotor1.ps1/screen2.ps1), vishing lock-screen overlays, phishing browser redirects, and CLABE/card-number clipboard hijacking via clip.ps1 and clip2.ps1.

item.title: Inside JADEPUFFER: Defending Against the First Agentic Ransomware
item.description:
JADEPUFFER is the first documented agentic ransomware, driven end to end by an LLM with no human operator. It exploited CVE-2025-3248 in an internet-facing Langflow instance, pivoted to production systems, and destroyed a MySQL database in a single autonomous run.
- CVE-2025-3248 is a missing-authentication vulnerability in Langflow. The agent used it for initial access, requiring no credentials. Internet-facing AI orchestration platforms are now a viable ransomware entry point, not just a misconfiguration risk.
- After gaining access, the agent pivoted to a production server and encrypted and destroyed both a MySQL database and a Nacos configuration service. No human operator directed the pivot or the targeting decisions.
- The agent self-healed mid-attack. When a login step failed, it diagnosed the error and corrected it autonomously in 31 seconds, machine-speed decision-making with no human in the loop.
- For DFIR, hunt for embedded LLM API keys in process memory or config files, and look for Langflow or similar AI orchestration services exposed to the internet. These are now lateral movement and persistence artifacts worth preserving.
Patch CVE-2025-3248 immediately and audit every internet-facing AI integration for authentication gaps. Behavioral detections need to account for attack chains with no human dwell time.

item.title: No Rules, No Locks: Firebase Misconfiguration and the Borrowers It Left Behind
item.description:
Firebase default-open rules exposed hundreds of Indonesian 🇮🇩 microfinance borrowers' full identity dossiers, GPS home coordinates, and biometric photos to unauthenticated REST access for at least five years.
Key findings:
- Entry point was /__/firebase/init.json, a public SDK config file every Firebase web app exposes by default. The projectId it contains is enough to construct REST endpoints for all three Firebase services: Storage, Firestore, and Realtime Database. No credentials, no browser, no session needed.
- Firebase Storage and Firestore both returned HTTP 200 to unauthenticated requests. Storage exposed 100+ files including versioned loan application schemas. Firestore's customers, loans, surveys, and groups collections were fully readable and writable. The Realtime Database alone returned 403.
- The surveys collection was the worst exposure: each document contained NIK (national ID), DOB, religion, mother's maiden name, husband's name, guarantor's NID, GPS coordinates, credit score, digital signature, and direct unauthenticated URLs to KTP photo, selfie, home photo, and signed loan PDF.
- Write and delete access was confirmed via the same unauthenticated API. An attacker could inject fake loan approvals, alter credit scores, or permanently delete financial records with no rate limiting and no audit trail.
Hunt: For any Firebase-backed app, pull /__/firebase/init.json, extract projectId, and test all three service endpoints unauthenticated.

item.title: The ‘Ghost’ in the Database: Recovering Active ADFS Signing Keys via Machine DPAPI
item.description:
Golden SAML lives on: Mandiant finds active ADFS token-signing keys recoverable via Machine DPAPI when AutoCertificateRollover is disabled and manual cert rotation leaves config drift.
Key findings:
- The "ghost certificate" trap: disabling AutoCertificateRollover and rotating certs manually without updating the WID database leaves a stale, unworkable cert in the DB. The real active signing key moves to C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Crypto\RSA\MachineKeys\, protected by Machine DPAPI using DPAPI_SYSTEM LSA secret plus S-1-5-18 masterkeys at C:\Windows\System32\Microsoft\Protect\S-1-5-18\. Standard DKM extraction returns the ghost; Entra ID rejects those tokens with AADSTS500172.
- SharpDPAPI /machine running as SYSTEM recovers the active RSA private key from the machine store, no LSASS touch, no live ADFS process interaction. Mandiant used it to forge a SAML assertion accepted by Entra ID at Global Administrator privilege across the federated M365 tenant.
- ADFS Event ID 385 is the canary: it flags certificate validity drift and is the observable symptom of this misconfiguration. Confirm with Get-AdfsProperties returning AutoCertificateRollover: False.
- Detection requires correlation: SACL-based Security Event ID 4663 on the MachineKeys and S-1-5-18 paths, cross-referenced with ADFS issuance events (299, 1200-series) and Entra ID federated sign-in logs. Neither source alone is sufficient.

item.title: Rogue Agent: How a Single Code Block Could Hijack Your AI Conversations in Google’s DialogFlow
item.description:
A single Dialogflow CX edit permission let attackers inject persistent Python into a shared Cloud Run environment, silently exfiltrating conversations and bypassing VPC Service Controls across an entire GCP project.
- The root cause: all Dialogflow CX agents sharing Code Blocks in a GCP project run inside the same Google-managed Cloud Run service. That environment had a writable filesystem, public egress, and no code execution restrictions. One permission, dialogflow.playbooks.update, was enough to overwrite code_execution_env.py, the file responsible for running Playbook Code Blocks via Python's exec() function, giving attackers full access to the history and state variables holding live conversation data and session parameters.
- The attack chain: a malicious Code Block downloads a trojaned code_execution_env.py from an attacker-controlled GCS bucket, overwrites the original, then the attacker restores the visible Code Block to look clean. The implant intercepts every subsequent user utterance, exfiltrates it externally, and can call respond() to inject phishing prompts that impersonate the legitimate agent. Cloud Logging recorded none of this.
- Two amplifying flaws: the Cloud Run environment sits outside VPC-SC perimeters, enabling data exfiltration even from VPC-SC-protected agents using standard urllib. IMDS was also reachable from within Code Blocks, exposing Google-managed service account tokens.
Google patched fully in June 2026.

item.title: Januscape: 16-Year-Old Linux KVM Bug Enables Cloud VM Escape Attacks
item.description:
CVE-2026-53359 "Januscape": a 16-year-old use-after-free in Linux KVM's shadow MMU lets a guest VM crash or potentially escape to the host, affecting both Intel and AMD x86 clouds exposing nested virtualization.
- CVE-2026-53359 lives in kvm_mmu_get_child_sp(), where KVM matched shadow page candidates by memory address alone, ignoring the page role type. A guest with root can race the shadow MMU until host kernel memory is corrupted. The public PoC reliably panics the host, taking every co-tenant VM down with it. A full code-execution exploit exists but has not been released.
- Attack prerequisites: root inside the guest (standard on any rented cloud VM) plus nested virtualization exposed by the host. The bug sits in in-kernel KVM, not QEMU, so custom cloud stacks that strip QEMU are not protected. GCP and AWS instances with nested virt enabled are the primary threat surface.
- On RHEL-family hosts where /dev/kvm is world-writable (0666), an unprivileged local user can trigger the bug without a VM at all, achieving host privilege escalation directly.
- Fixed kernel versions shipped July 4, 2026: 7.1.3, 6.18.38, 6.12.95, 6.6.144, 6.1.177, 5.15.211, and 5.10.260, via commit 81ccda30b4e8. No CVSS score assigned yet.
Confirm commit 81ccda30b4e8 in your running kernel via package changelog, not uname -r, as distro backports may differ. If patching is blocked, set kvm_intel.nested=0 or kvm_amd.nested=0 immediately to eliminate the guest-to-host path.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2074524712819167698

item.title: Banana RAT Evolves: Comparing Two Recent Branches Through ANY.RUN
item.description:
Banana RAT operator exposed via open server index, revealing two live branches and a FastAPI payload generator, showing deliberate evolution in persistence, transport, and artifact naming between May and June 2026.

item.title: The HTTP 303 SSRF Hack : From Python HTTP Client Defaults to AWS Credential Exfiltration.
item.description:
A blind SSRF escalated to live AWS IAM credential theft by chaining a user-controlled OAuth field, Python requests default redirect handling, and IMDSv1 reachability on an EKS node. No single component was broken. The composition was.
- BigQuery service account JSON accepted by the platform contained a user-supplied token_uri field with zero allowlist validation. The backend passed it verbatim to the google-auth library, which POSTed a signed JWT to whatever URL the attacker provided. An OOB Interactsh probe confirmed the primitive immediately.
- Direct SSRF to 169.254.169[.]254 failed because IMDS returns HTTP 405 to POST requests. Timing analysis (IMDS responded in 0.34s vs. 28s for an unroutable IP) proved the pod could reach IMDS, the verb was simply wrong. The fix: serve HTTP 303 See Other from an attacker-controlled server. Per RFC 7231 §6.4.4, Python requests rewrites POST to GET on a 303, strips the body, and follows the Location header to IMDS.
- The error reflection channel completed the read primitive. google-auth parsed the IMDS JSON response, failed to find access_token, raised an exception, and the worker returned the raw exception string, including AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken, in the HTTP 400 body to the authenticated caller.
- Remediation: the platform implemented a frozenset allowlist at the field-parsing layer, blocking any token_uri not matching oauth2.googleapis[.]com/token or accounts.google[.]com/o/oauth2/token.

item.description:

item.title: The File That Answered Back — XXE Hidden in Cell A2
item.description:

item.title: Hack the Elephant One Bite at a Time: NUL byte SQL Injection in pdo_firebird and NULL Pointer Dereference in PDO via pdo_pgsql
item.description:
Two PHP PDO bugs patched in 2025-2026: CVE-2025-14179 enables SQL injection via NUL bytes in pdo_firebird, and CVE-2025-14180 causes a NULL pointer dereference crash in pdo_pgsql, both rooted in unsafe C-level input handling.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-14179 (High) hits pdo_firebird's php_firebird_preprocess tokenizer. The quoting routine PDO::quote works correctly, but when the rebuilt SQL string passes through php_firebird_alloc_prepare_stmt, a strncat() call truncates on the first NUL byte (\0), dropping the closing quote of a string literal. Attacker input escapes the quoted context and is parsed as executable SQL. The exploit pattern: quote with PDO::quote, pass to PDO::prepare, inject \0 in the first parameter, then place a UNION SELECT payload in the second. Fixed in commit 3f40b65 by replacing strncat() with a binary-safe length-bounded copy.
- CVE-2025-14180 (Moderate, CVSS 6.3) affects pdo_pgsql when PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES is true. A parameter containing an invalid multibyte sequence (e.g. alice\x99) causes libpq's PQescapeStringConn to set the error flag and the driver returns NULL. The PDO parser then evaluates ZSTR_LEN(NULL), dereferencing address 0x0, delivering SIGSEGV and killing the PHP worker instantly. The try/catch block never fires because the crash is at C level.
- The DoS has real financial impact. In autocommit mode, a debit UPDATE commits before the crash point, but the order INSERT, inventory UPDATE, and invoice INSERT never run.

item.title: Exploiting Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD)
item.description:
RBCD exploitation gives any user with write access to a computer object a clear path to full machine takeover via Kerberos delegation abuse, no Domain Admin required.
Key details:
- The attack abuses msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on the target computer object. Any principal with write rights over that attribute, including the object's creator, can configure RBCD. Default MachineAccountQuota lets any authenticated user add up to 10 computer accounts, supplying a ready-made SPN-bearing "Service A" with no special privileges needed.
- The chain: create a rogue computer account (addcomputer.py or Powermad), write RBCD trust to the target with rbcd.py, call S4U2Self to get a non-forwardable ticket for Administrator, then S4U2Proxy to exchange it for a cifs ticket, and pass it with psexec.py, secretsdump.py, or smbclient.py.
- RBCD's critical difference from classic constrained delegation: the KDC accepts a non-forwardable evidence ticket as long as the target resource's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity trusts the requestor, bypassing the FORWARDABLE check that blocks classic delegation abuse.
- Artifact focus: query AD for unexpected values in msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on workstations and servers, and audit newly created computer accounts (Event ID 4741). Rubeus and getST.py leave Kerberos S4U activity in KDC logs (Event ID 4769) with unusual delegation fields.

item.title: The Blind Spot in the Watchtower: Detections for When Someone Attacks Your Sentinel
item.description:
Microsoft Sentinel has no built-in watch over itself: nine KQL detections close the blind spot attackers exploit to disable rules, cut log feeds, and erase their own incidents before any alert fires.
Most SOC teams have hundreds of detections aimed outward at endpoints, email, and identity. Almost none watch the SIEM itself. A capable attacker does not start loud. They reach for the recorder first.
- Sentinel stores its own audit trail across three tables: AzureActivity (free, all resource changes), _SentinelAudit() (rule-level before/after diff, requires health and audit feature enabled), and _SentinelHealth() (confirms rules are actually running). item.description:

- Email rules now gate domain exemptions on coalesce(headers.auth_summary.dmarc.pass, false), so brand impersonation bypasses via spoofed high-trust domains lose their exception. item.title: PamStealer: a Rust-based macOS infostealer that validates credentials through PAM
item.description:
PamStealer, a Rust-based macOS 🍎 infostealer disguised as the Maccy clipboard manager, uses PAM to silently validate stolen credentials before exfiltrating browser data, keychain secrets, and clipboard contents.
Key findings:
- Stage 1 drops a trojanized Maccy app bundle. The malicious payload is a Rust binary embedded inside a legitimate-looking .app, making static detection harder since Rust binaries strip cleanly and carry little metadata for signature-based tools to anchor on.
- Stage 2 abuses the PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) framework to verify harvested credentials in real time before exfil, a technique that confirms credential validity on the victim machine without touching an external service and reducing noise.
- Targets include browser-stored credentials, clipboard contents, and macOS keychain data, giving the attacker a broad credential harvest from a single execution.
- The disguise as Maccy, a popular open-source clipboard utility, suggests delivery via trojanized downloads or typosquatting, targeting macOS users who actively seek clipboard tools.
DFIR takeaway: on macOS endpoints, examine LaunchAgents and LaunchDaemons for unsigned or recently added entries, and check for unexpected PAM API calls in unified logs via log show filtering on pam_authenticate. item.title: Chaining an Apache ActiveMQ RCE on a Fully Patched 6.2.5 (CVE-2026-34197)
item.description:
CVE-2026-34197: A two-bug chain achieves post-auth RCE on fully patched Apache ActiveMQ Classic 6.2.5 on Windows, bypassing both the URI validator and the XBean protocol allowlist with a single Jolokia call.
- CVE-2026-34197 is a post-auth RCE via the Jolokia endpoint: an authenticated call to BrokerView.addNetworkConnector with a vm:// URI carrying a brokerConfig=xbean: parameter causes the broker to load attacker-controlled Spring XML and instantiate a ProcessBuilder bean. The 6.2.5 patch added a deny-list validator and locked XBeanBrokerFactory to file,classpath protocols. Both controls fail.
- Bug 1 (validator bypass): validateAllowedUri only recurses into composite URI components when isCompositeURI returns true, which requires the scheme-specific part to start with "(". Prefixing the payload with bare static: (no parens) passes the outer scheme check and skips recursion entirely, so the inner vm:// is never inspected.
- Bug 2 (allowlist bypass): The allowlist blocks file:// as a remote path, but the classifier uses raw String.startsWith on the undecoded URI. Percent-encoding the slashes (file:%2525252f%2525252f...) makes the classifier see a plain local file: scheme while the JDK decodes it back to file://HOST/SHARE at open time. On Windows this resolves as a UNC path; with 445/TCP closed on the attacker side, the Windows WebDAV redirector (WebClient service) fetches the payload over HTTP, no credentials needed.

item.title: Missed incidents, persistent threats, and response gaps: Insights from compromise assessment projects
item.description:
Kaspersky's 2025 compromise assessment data reveals a systemic detection failure: 60% of incidents were missed entirely by existing tools, 52% of high-severity compromises went undetected for over 90 days, and one incident had persisted for four years.
Key findings:
- Dwell time drives severity. Incidents detected within 30 days show balanced severity distribution. By 60-90 days, 71% are high-severity. Beyond 90 days, 52% are still high-severity. The four-year case involved NSABuffMiner crypto-mining on domain controllers via EternalBlue (MS17-010), with malicious files hidden in C:\Windows\Fonts\Mysql and persistence via services named MicrosoftMysql and MicrosoftFonts, plus scheduled tasks At1 and At2.
- Post-IR checkups produced the highest proportion of high-severity findings (40.7%), exposing what contained IR misses. One case found a cron job re-downloading a PHP web shell from GitHub, a live bash reverse shell running as the apache user, a ClipBanker variant persisting under HKU\...\Run\9Er6IIp, and a WMI event consumer aliasing Invoke-Expression as "Kaspersky."
- 40% of discovered web shells lived in backups. Asset inventory gaps (25% of engagements) meant cloud Linux servers outside AD never got scanned, and backup restores reintroduced the threat repeatedly.
- Without 24/7 monitoring or threat hunting, 84-86% of incidents were medium or high severity.

item.title: FortiBleed: Inside the Campaign That Cracked 75,000 Fortinet Firewalls
item.description:
FortiBleed: verified admin and SSL VPN credentials for ~75,000 internet-facing FortiGate firewalls leaked across 194 countries, with no CVE and no patch available.
Key findings:
- No vulnerability to patch here. FortiBleed stems from stolen device configs, credential reuse, and offline cracking of legacy SHA-256 password hashes. FortiGate management interfaces exposed to the internet were the entry point, and the weak hashing did the rest.
- PBKDF2 stronger hashing only activates after each admin re-authenticates. Devices where admins have not logged in since the upgrade still store crackable SHA-256 hashes, meaning the exposure persists silently on patched devices.
- IT services and telecoms are hit hardest, but affected orgs span every sector across 194 countries. Scale matters here: 75,000 firewalls with working credentials is a ready-made access broker inventory.
- No CVE means no patch Tuesday trigger and no automatic alerting. Defenders must act without a traditional vulnerability remediation workflow.
Takeaway: pull your FortiGate management interface off the internet now, force all admins to re-authenticate to trigger PBKDF2 re-hashing, and enable MFA on all admin and VPN accounts. Hunt for any management interface still internet-exposed using your asset inventory and verify FortiOS is current.

item.title: RustDuck: The Botnet That’s Still Small but Engineering Like It Plans to Grow
item.description:
RustDuck botnet targets IoT and servers with Rust-rewritten malware, layered C2 encryption, and a weighted anti-sandbox scoring system, signaling rapid capability growth from a still-small but technically ambitious operation tracked since February 2026.
Key details:
- Entry points span default Telnet/SSH creds, Android ADB, DVRs from TVT, routers from Ruijie, TP-Link, ZTE, plus ThinkPHP, Jenkins, and Hadoop YARN. CVEs include CVE-2025-29635 (CISA KEV, D-Link DIR-823X command injection, no patch, retire it), CVE-2017-17215 (Huawei HG532 RCE, Mirai-era), CVE-2024-1781 (Totolink X6000R, unpatched), and CVE-2018-8007 (Apache CouchDB admin RCE).
- The loader chain has cycled through four encryption schemes: LCG+XOR+LZ4, Xoshiro128 with hardcoded constants, XOR with a fixed magic string, and now ChaCha20. Each iteration was a direct response to analyst detection, not coincidence.
- Anti-analysis scoring assigns 100 points each for detecting Wireshark, gdb, or Frida in the process list, a debugger in /proc/self/status, or a tampered file checksum; 50 for Cowrie/Dionaea honeypot files; 35 for a response from 192.0.2.1. A dual-clock timing check catches sandboxes that accelerate execution. Exceed the threshold and the malware self-erases.
- C2 uses ChaCha20-Poly1305 with Curve25519 key exchange and HKDF-SHA256 derivation, keys rotating every 10 minutes, then switches to AES-GCM with split up/down keys. A three-byte header mimics TLS records.

item.title: Hack Smarter — City Council (Active Directory)
item.description:

- Credential recovery from a WIM profile backup exposed emma.hayes plaintext creds stored in PowerShell history (ConsoleHost_history.txt) as a cmdkey command, a classic artifact defenders routinely miss.
- emma.hayes WriteDacl on CityOps OU escalated to GenericAll, enabling account re-enabling and password reset of sam.brooks (Remote Management Users) for WinRM access, then web_admin for IIS write access.

item.title: Azure CLI Targeted in LSHIY Password Spray Campaign Across 64 Orgs
item.description:
An ongoing password spray campaign abusing Azure CLI's OAuth ROPC flow has compromised 78 accounts across 64 orgs in 14 days, defeating MFA at 15 of 23 businesses hit on a single day.
Key findings:
- 81 million login attempts since June 12, 2026, sourced almost entirely from IPv6 range 2a0a:d683[.]/32, tied to LSHIY LLC (AS32167/AS955), with third parties linking both ASNs to Chinese 🇨🇳 infrastructure. LSHIY lists addresses in Hong Kong 🇭🇰 and Wuhan alongside a New York 🇺🇸 shared office.
- Attack method: threat actors replay breach-dump credentials against the OAuth 2.0 ROPC /token endpoint. Because ROPC sends credentials directly and never hits the authorization endpoint, Conditional Access Policies enforcing MFA do not fire, making it an effective MFA bypass.
- 15 of 23 companies hit on June 22 had MFA via CAP and were still compromised. Root causes: MFA scoped to admin portals only, trusted-location rules that the attackers' inconsistently geolocated IPs bypassed, and two orgs running CAP in report-only mode.
- Huntress reports credential spray volume across its customer base has grown 155x in six months, averaging roughly 1,964 failed attempts per protected tenant per month.
Remediation: scope your Conditional Access Policy to all users, all cloud apps, all client app types. Enable userStrongAuthClientAuthNRequired to block ROPC outright. On detection, triage by credential validity rather than raw spray volume.

item.title: CVE-2026-48558: SimpleHelp OIDC Auth Bypass Used to Deploy Infostealer Payloads
item.description:
CVE-2026-48558 in SimpleHelp allows unauthenticated attackers to forge OIDC tokens, seize technician sessions, and deploy Djinn Stealer across managed endpoints. CISA KEV-listed with a July 2 remediation deadline.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-48558 is a cryptographic signature validation failure in SimpleHelp's OIDC login flow. The server accepts forged identity tokens without verifying the signature, handing an unauthenticated attacker a full technician session. Affected versions: 5.5.1 through 5.5.15 and 6.0 pre-release builds before 6.0 RC2. Fix: upgrade to 5.5.16+ or 6.0 RC2+.
- Exploitation is conditional: you are only exposed if OIDC is enabled AND Technician Groups are configured with "Allow group authenticated logins." If OIDC is off entirely, this bypass does not apply.
- Active exploitation delivers TaskWeaver, an obfuscated Node.js loader masquerading as jquery.js and executed as "node.exe jquery.js", followed by Djinn Stealer, a cross-platform infostealer targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux. Targets include browser credentials, SSH keys, cloud tokens, and developer secrets.
- In MSP environments, one compromised technician session is a pivot point into every downstream customer. The blast radius is not one host; it is the entire managed estate.
